subject: Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data

messages.author: b8a1da45c9a2eab1
messages.subject: Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data
parts:
Dear All,

 

I am analysing some seabird line transect data using distance methods in R. The data were collected from a ship using standard European Seabirds at Sea Methods (Webb, A. and J. Durinck (1992). Counting birds from ships. Manual for aeroplane and ship surveys of waterfowl and seabirds. IWRB Special Publication. 19: 24-37). In brief, detections are binned at the time of collection into one of four distance bands, bounded by 0-50, 50-100, 100-200 and 200-300 m.

 

As the data are binned, I planned to assess goodness of fit of potential detection functions using chi-square tests. Eric Rexstad points out in a previous exchange on this list that “degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is defined as u-q-1, where u is the number of bins and q is the number of parameters in the detection function”. With only four bins, I am therefore considered to consider only detection functions containing two or less parameters. However, I have a relatively large sample size (n = 711 clusters). This means that the chi-square test tends to indicate significant discrepancies between my candidate detection functions and the data, an issue that has previously been eluded to here

 

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distancesampling/chi$20square$20large$20sample%Csort:date/distance-sampling/rf4DlB_ihS4/YIRBQiQnrFMJ

 

and by Buckland et al. 2015 (section 5.1.4). For example, when I fit a half-normal function with two cosine adjustments to my full data set, the p value for chi-square is 0.006. The same function fitted to a randomly thinned data set of n = 100 results in p = 0.698 for chi-sq.

 

That being the case, which of the approach to assessing goodness of fit is recommended? (1) Thin the data prior to fitting the detection function and use chi-sq to assess model fit? This seems like a waste of data and would force an arbitrary choice of n. Or (2) use the full data set and simply assess model fit visually, as recommended here:

 

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/degrees$20of$20freedom%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/upAAXToeCVI/x9NKqQlVAQAJ

 

If approach #2 is preferred, does that mean that it would then be valid to consider models with >2 parameters or should I still constrain my field of candidate models to those with <= 2 parameters (and if so why?!)

 

Thanks in advance for your assistance.

 

Ewan Wakefield

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data
parts:
Ewan

Glad to see you are paying close attention to model fit diagnostics.  You are correct in all the material you pointed out, with minor exception that the model yuo fitted must have been a half-normal with a *single* adjustment term of order 2 (had it been HN with 2 adjustments you would have a model with 3 parameters, hence no degrees of freedom left for goodness of fit testing).

Your conundrum is how to proceed with GOF testing with binned data with few bins.  This is a matter of some personal preference and others might not agree with my opinion.  I would not use the "random filtering" as it seems artificial.  The purpose of the GOF testing is to assess the validity of the model you are using in the inference you are making about the population estimate.  I would show the reader of your report the chosen detection function superimposed upon the histogram of the data, as produced by the gof_ds() function.  I would also speak to the subject of model fit in your results section, but I would not feel compelled to produce a test statistic in the circumstances you describe.  This is akin to the option (2) you present.

Following on with the second part of your question, conditional upon the adoption of option (2), could you be more expansive in the range of candidate models.  Recognise that option (2) only "buys" you a single degree of freedom, permitting your universe of candidate models to have (perhaps) a half-normal key with 2 adjustments.  I would not expect this to make much practical difference.  In theory we expect detection functions to be fairly smooth, I think it would be unusual for there to be two changes in derivatives (bumps) in a histogram that has only 4 points of support (bins).  That might be over-fitting to the data rather than fitting to the process that gave rise to the data.  I would restrain my enthusiasm for fitting a 3 parameter model to data with 4 points of support, even if I was not constrained to "saving" a degree of freedom for testing of fit.

messages.author: b8a1da45c9a2eab1
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data
parts: Thanks for your constructive reply, Eric.
>with minor exception that the model yuo fitted must have been a half-normal with a *single* adjustment term of order 2

Correct - that was a typo. In the first instance, I also fitted a uniform function with two cosine adjustments; a half-normal with one Hermite polynomial adjustment; and a hazard rate function with no adjustments. The latter has the lowest AIC and best fit according to the chi-sq test.
>Following on with the second part of your question, conditional upon the adoption of option (2), could you be more expansive in the range of candidate models.

In addition to the candidate models described above, exploratory analysis suggests that a whole suite of covariates affect the rate of decay of the detection function. These include sea state and wind speed (which are obviously colinear so I wouldn't consider both in the same model), cluster size and observer. Based on your reply, it seems reasonable that I could consider a half-normal model (with no adjustments) and parameters for wind speed (or sea state) and cluster size, as well as sub-models contained therein.  Observer has eight levels so I presume that this there's no way that this covaraite could also be considered. Am I right that the only option for capturing variation due to observer with my data set would be stratify by observer? Presumably, the alternative would be to trust that pooling robustness deals with inter-observer variability?

All the best,

Ewan

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re[2]: [distance-sampling] Assessing detection function goodness of fit with large sample size and binned data
parts: Yes, Ewan, I agree with your conjectures.  You would not be able to explore covariates treated as factors unless there were a restricted number of levels.  I suppose you could stratify by observer, but putting those estimates back together into an overall estimate would be complicated.  Pooling robustness does give you the ability to rely upon an unbiased estimate even in the face of unmodelled differences in detectability due to observer.
